name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMAL_KINGDOM_MCQ_Q01 - Distinctive diagnostic structures of invertebrate phyla

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Characteristic Structure) List-II (Phylum)
A. Choanocytes I. Ctenophora
B. Cnidoblasts II. Mollusca
C. Comb plates III. Porifera
D. Radula IV. Coelenterata

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Choanocytes, or collar cells, line the spongocoel and internal canals of sponges, which belong to the phylum Porifera. They maintain water flow, capture food particles, and assist in respiratory exchange.

Step 2:
Cnidoblasts (cnidocytes) contain stinging capsules termed nematocysts and are located on the tentacles and body wall of organisms in the phylum Coelenterata (Cnidaria), where they function in anchorage, defense, and prey capture.

Step 3:
Comb plates consist of eight external rows of fused, ciliated plates uniquely characteristic of the phylum Ctenophora, serving specifically as locomotor organs.

Step 4:
The radula is a specialized file-like rasping organ situated in the buccal cavity of animals in the phylum Mollusca, utilized to scrape and fragment food.

Step 5:
Correlating each structure with its representative phylum establishes that Choanocytes correspond to Porifera, Cnidoblasts correspond to Coelenterata, Comb plates correspond to Ctenophora, and Radula corresponds to Mollusca.

Final Answer:
Choanocytes match with Porifera, Cnidoblasts match with Coelenterata, Comb plates match with Ctenophora, and Radula matches with Mollusca (A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMAL_KINGDOM_MCQ_Q02 - Arthropod classification based on economic importance

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Category / Ecological Role) List-II (Arthropod Example)
A. Economically important insect I. Locusta
B. Disease vector II. Limulus
C. Gregarious pest III. Apis
D. Living fossil IV. Anopheles

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
The honey bee, belonging to the genus Apis, produces commercial honey and beeswax, thereby serving as an economically important insect.

Step 2:
The mosquito Anopheles transmits the malaria-causing protozoan parasite between human hosts, functioning directly as a biological disease vector.

Step 3:
Locusts, belonging to the genus Locusta, congregate in large migratory swarms that severely damage agricultural crops, classifying them as gregarious pests.

Step 4:
The king crab, Limulus, has survived essentially unchanged over hundreds of millions of years without close living relatives, representing a classic living fossil.

Step 5:
Matching each ecological role with its corresponding arthropod reveals that Economically important insect corresponds to Apis, Disease vector corresponds to Anopheles, Gregarious pest corresponds to Locusta, and Living fossil corresponds to Limulus.

Final Answer:
Economically important insect matches with Apis, Disease vector matches with Anopheles, Gregarious pest matches with Locusta, and Living fossil matches with Limulus (A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMAL_KINGDOM_MCQ_Q03 - Excretory structures across diverse animal phyla

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Excretory / Osmoregulatory Structure) List-II (Animal Example)
A. Flame cells I. Locusta
B. Nephridia II. Balanoglossus
C. Malpighian tubules III. Fasciola
D. Proboscis gland IV. Pheretima

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Flame cells (solenocytes) are specialized ciliated excretory and osmoregulatory cells characteristic of the flatworm Fasciola (liver fluke) in the phylum Platyhelminthes.

Step 2:
Nephridia are tubular coiled structures responsible for osmoregulation and excretion in segmented annelids, such as the earthworm Pheretima.

Step 3:
Malpighian tubules are slender excretory structures situated at the junction of the midgut and hindgut in terrestrial arthropods, such as the locust Locusta.

Step 4:
The proboscis gland (glomerulus) is an excretory organ located in the anterior proboscis region of hemichordates, including the acorn worm Balanoglossus.

Step 5:
Integrating these associations verifies that Flame cells pair with Fasciola, Nephridia pair with Pheretima, Malpighian tubules pair with Locusta, and Proboscis gland pairs with Balanoglossus.

Final Answer:
Flame cells match with Fasciola, Nephridia match with Pheretima, Malpighian tubules match with Locusta, and Proboscis gland matches with Balanoglossus (A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMAL_KINGDOM_MCQ_Q04 - Scientific and common names of cnidarians

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Scientific Name) List-II (Common Name)
A. Physalia I. Sea anemone
B. Adamsia II. Sea-pen
C. Pennatula III. Sea-fan
D. Gorgonia IV. Portuguese man-of-war

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Physalia is a polymorphic colonial cnidarian featuring a large gas-filled pneumatophore that resembles an armed sailing ship, commonly referred to as the Portuguese man-of-war.

Step 2:
Adamsia is a sessile, solitary polyp that frequently forms a mutualistic association with hermit crabs, commonly called the sea anemone.

Step 3:
Pennatula is a colonial anthozoan whose fleshy axial stalk and lateral branchlets give it a quill-like appearance, earning the common name sea-pen.

Step 4:
Gorgonia forms a flattened, fan-shaped branched colonial skeleton composed of gorgonin, commonly known as the sea-fan.

Step 5:
Aligning these taxa with their established common names confirms that Physalia corresponds to Portuguese man-of-war, Adamsia corresponds to Sea anemone, Pennatula corresponds to Sea-pen, and Gorgonia corresponds to Sea-fan.

Final Answer:
Physalia matches with Portuguese man-of-war, Adamsia matches with Sea anemone, Pennatula matches with Sea-pen, and Gorgonia matches with Sea-fan (A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMAL_KINGDOM_MCQ_Q05 - Fundamental anatomical criteria in animal classification

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Animal Group) List-II (Level, Symmetry, and Coelom Status)
A. Sponges I. Triploblastic, bilateral symmetry, pseudocoelomate
B. Platyhelminthes II. Triploblastic, bilateral symmetry, true coelomate
C. Aschelminthes III. Cellular level, mostly asymmetrical, acoelomate
D. Annelids IV. Triploblastic, bilateral symmetry, acoelomate

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Sponges (phylum Porifera) possess a cellular level of body organization with loose cell aggregates, lack true germ layers, are mostly asymmetrical, and lack any body cavity (acoelomate).

Step 2:
Flatworms (phylum Platyhelminthes) exhibit organ and organ-system levels of organization, possess bilateral symmetry, develop from three embryonic germ layers (triploblastic), but lack a body cavity between the body wall and gut (acoelomate).

Step 3:
Roundworms (phylum Aschelminthes) display an organ-system level of organization, are triploblastic and bilaterally symmetrical, and possess a body cavity in which mesoderm is present as scattered pouches rather than a continuous peritoneal lining, defining the pseudocoelomate state.

Step 4:
Annelids (phylum Annelida) are triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical, metamerically segmented animals possessing a true secondary body cavity entirely lined by mesoderm (coelomate).

Step 5:
Synthesizing these fundamental body plans confirms that Sponges pair with Cellular level, mostly asymmetrical, acoelomate; Platyhelminthes pair with Triploblastic, bilateral symmetry, acoelomate; Aschelminthes pair with Triploblastic, bilateral symmetry, pseudocoelomate; and Annelids pair with Triploblastic, bilateral symmetry, true coelomate.

Final Answer:
Sponges match with Cellular level, mostly asymmetrical, acoelomate; Platyhelminthes match with Triploblastic, bilateral symmetry, acoelomate; Aschelminthes match with Triploblastic, bilateral symmetry, pseudocoelomate; and Annelids match with Triploblastic, bilateral symmetry, true coelomate (A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMAL_KINGDOM_MCQ_Q06 - Molluscan genera paired with common names

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Molluscan Genus) List-II (Common Name)
A. Pinctada I. Cuttlefish
B. Sepia II. Sea-hare
C. Aplysia III. Tusk shell
D. Dentalium IV. Pearl oyster

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Pinctada is a marine bivalve mollusc widely known for nacre secretion around foreign particles to produce genuine pearls, earning it the common name pearl oyster.

Step 2:
Sepia is a decapod cephalopod possessing an internal porous aragonite shell (cuttlebone) and an ink sac, commonly termed cuttlefish.

Step 3:
Aplysia is an opisthobranch marine gastropod with prominent anterior tentacular rhinophores resembling the ears of a hare, commonly called the sea-hare.

Step 4:
Dentalium belongs to the molluscan class Scaphopoda and builds an elongated, gently curved, tubular shell open at both ends, commonly named the tusk shell.

Step 5:
Correlating each genus with its common name proves that Pinctada corresponds to Pearl oyster, Sepia corresponds to Cuttlefish, Aplysia corresponds to Sea-hare, and Dentalium corresponds to Tusk shell.

Final Answer:
Pinctada matches with Pearl oyster, Sepia matches with Cuttlefish, Aplysia matches with Sea-hare, and Dentalium matches with Tusk shell (A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMAL_KINGDOM_MCQ_Q07 - Characteristic features of chordate subphyla and classes

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Taxonomic Group) List-II (Diagnostic Feature)
A. Urochordata I. Notochord extends from head to tail and persists throughout life
B. Cephalochordata II. Sucking circular mouth without jaws, cartilaginous cranium
C. Cyclostomata III. Notochord present only in larval tail
D. Chondrichthyes IV. Cartilaginous endoskeleton with persistent notochord and placoid scales

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
In subphylum Urochordata (tunicates like Ascidia), the notochord is strictly restricted to the tail of the free-swimming larva and is completely lost in the adult during retrogressive metamorphosis.

Step 2:
In subphylum Cephalochordata (lancelets like Branchiostoma), the notochord extends along the entire length of the animal from the anterior head tip to the posterior tail tip and persists unchanged throughout life.

Step 3:
Class Cyclostomata comprises primitive, jawless vertebrates characterized by a circular and sucking mouth, absence of paired fins and scales, and a cartilaginous cranium and vertebral column.

Step 4:
Class Chondrichthyes comprises marine cartilaginous fishes whose notochord remains persistent throughout life, with tough skin covered by backwardly directed placoid scales and gill slits lacking an operculum.

Step 5:
Combining these chordate diagnostic criteria confirms that Urochordata corresponds to notochord present only in larval tail, Cephalochordata corresponds to notochord extending from head to tail throughout life, Cyclostomata corresponds to sucking circular mouth without jaws and cartilaginous cranium, and Chondrichthyes corresponds to cartilaginous endoskeleton with persistent notochord and placoid scales.

Final Answer:
Urochordata matches with notochord present only in larval tail, Cephalochordata matches with notochord extending from head to tail throughout life, Cyclostomata matches with sucking circular mouth without jaws and cartilaginous cranium, and Chondrichthyes matches with cartilaginous endoskeleton with persistent notochord and placoid scales (A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMAL_KINGDOM_MCQ_Q08 - Diagnostic adaptations of aquatic and amphibian vertebrates

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Organism) List-II (Specialized Adaptation / Trait)
A. Torpedo I. Poison sting on tail
B. Trygon II. Electric organ
C. Exocoetus III. Limbless amphibian
D. Ichthyophis IV. Flying fish

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Torpedo is an electric ray belonging to class Chondrichthyes that possesses modified branchial muscular tissue capable of delivering defensive and predatory electric shocks (electric organ).

Step 2:
Trygon is a stingray belonging to class Chondrichthyes that possesses a serrated, venomous spine on its whip-like tail (poison sting).

Step 3:
Exocoetus is an osteichthyan marine bony fish with unusually large wing-like pectoral fins that enable prolonged gliding flights out of the water, commonly termed the flying fish.

Step 4:
Ichthyophis is a specialized, subterranean burrowing member of class Amphibia that has secondarily lost both pairs of limbs, representing a limbless amphibia.

Step 5:
Evaluating all adaptations confirms that Torpedo matches with Electric organ, Trygon matches with Poison sting on tail, Exocoetus matches with Flying fish, and Ichthyophis matches with Limbless amphibian.

Final Answer:
Torpedo matches with Electric organ, Trygon matches with Poison sting on tail, Exocoetus matches with Flying fish, and Ichthyophis matches with Limbless amphibian (A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMAL_KINGDOM_MCQ_Q09 - Locomotor and respiratory adaptations in non-chordate phyla

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Organism) List-II (Organ of Locomotion / Respiration)
A. Nereis I. Ciliated comb plates for locomotion
B. Pleurobrachia II. Lateral appendages (parapodia) for swimming
C. Asterias III. Water vascular system aiding locomotion and respiration
D. Pila IV. Feather-like gills in mantle cavity for respiration and excretion

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Nereis is an aquatic polychaete annelid whose lateral unjointed fleshy appendages, termed parapodia, are adapted for swimming and cutaneous gas exchange.

Step 2:
Pleurobrachia is a ctenophore possessing eight external longitudinal rows of fused cilia known as comb plates, which serve as its primary locomotor apparatus.

Step 3:
Asterias (starfish) is an echinoderm possessing a distinctive hydraulic water vascular system that drives ambulacral tube feet for locomotion, food transport, and gas exchange.

Step 4:
Pila (apple snail) is a mollusc that bears ctenidia (feather-like gills) inside its mantle cavity, executing dual respiratory and excretory functions.

Step 5:
Matching these physiological structures verifies that Nereis corresponds to Lateral appendages (parapodia) for swimming, Pleurobrachia corresponds to Ciliated comb plates for locomotion, Asterias corresponds to Water vascular system, and Pila corresponds to Feather-like gills in mantle cavity.

Final Answer:
Nereis matches with Lateral appendages (parapodia) for swimming, Pleurobrachia matches with Ciliated comb plates for locomotion, Asterias matches with Water vascular system, and Pila matches with Feather-like gills in mantle cavity (A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMAL_KINGDOM_MCQ_Q10 - Distinguishing anatomical traits of higher vertebrate classes

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Vertebrate Class) List-II (Combination of Diagnostic Traits)
A. Reptilia I. Fully ossified skeleton with pneumatic bones, crop and gizzard, homoiothermous
B. Aves II. Dry cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes, poikilothermous, internal fertilisation
C. Mammalia III. Mammary glands for nourishing young, pinnae, hair, mostly viviparous
D. Osteichthyes IV. Four pairs of gills with operculum, air bladder present, terminal mouth

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1:
Members of class Reptilia are creeping terrestrial vertebrates covered by dry, cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes, lack external ear openings (tympanum represents ear), are poikilothermous, and exhibit internal fertilisation with oviparous direct development.

Step 2:
Members of class Aves possess feathers, forelimbs modified into wings, hollow pneumatic bones containing air cavities, an alimentary canal with specialized crop and gizzard chambers, fully four-chambered hearts, and homoiothermy.

Step 3:
Members of class Mammalia are distinguished by functional mammary glands that produce milk, skin possessing hair, external ear pinnae, four-chambered hearts, homoiothermy, and predominantly viviparous reproduction.

Step 4:
Members of class Osteichthyes possess a bony endoskeleton, streamlined body with a mostly terminal mouth, four pairs of gill slits covered by an operculum on each side, cycloid or ctenoid scales, and a gas-filled air bladder that regulates buoyancy.

Step 5:
Comparing these diagnostic trait complexes confirms that Reptilia corresponds to dry cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes; Aves corresponds to fully ossified skeleton with pneumatic bones, crop and gizzard; Mammalia corresponds to mammary glands, pinnae, hair; and Osteichthyes corresponds to four pairs of gills with operculum and air bladder.

Final Answer:
Reptilia matches with dry cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes, poikilothermous, internal fertilisation; Aves matches with fully ossified skeleton with pneumatic bones, crop and gizzard, homoiothermous; Mammalia matches with mammary glands for nourishing young, pinnae, hair, mostly viviparous; and Osteichthyes matches with four pairs of gills with operculum, air bladder present, terminal mouth (A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV).
